prompt.context: The client is a private equity firm looking to acquire a chain of car washes in the United States. The car wash chain provides basic coin-operated, self-wash services for $5, has 200 locations in 14 markets and had revenues of $40M last year. The firm is targeting 30% revenue growth in 1 year to justify the acquisition.
prompt.question: How would you think about whether or not this 30% revenue growth target is attainable?

clarifying_info.q: Has the firm explored increasing sales of existing products and services in existing markets?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, that has already been explored and is not a viable option.

exhibits.title: Existing Markets and Competitors
exhibits.shows: A map or table of the chain's 14 existing markets showing the chain's market share position relative to national and local competitors in each market
exhibits.data: Market share rankings across 14 markets; presence or absence of competing national chains; geographic distribution of locations

framework: 1. Existing Locations — New Products/Services: assess customer demand, price sensitivity, changing hours, marketing, advertising, partnerships, social media
1. Existing Locations — Increase Price: evaluate price sensitivity of current customer base
2. New Locations — Existing Markets: expand within current 14 markets by acquiring or driving out local competitors
2. New Locations — New Markets: enter untapped geographies (Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, Southwest)
3. Risks — Over-extended management from rapid expansion
3. Risks — Cost implications of adding services or locations (note: primary concern is revenue)

questions.prompt: What do you think is the size of the car wash market as a whole in the United States?
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate number of vehicles, frequency of washes, and average price per wash. Reasonable assumptions are acceptable; the interviewer is evaluating structured estimation, not a precise number.

math.setup: Number of vehicles × washes per year × average price per wash
steps: Estimate 20 washes per vehicle per year (10–20 is reasonable)
math.answer: $16.5 billion total US car wash market

questions.prompt: Look at Exhibit 1 showing the chain's existing 14 markets and competitors. What do you gather from it?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) the chain holds highest market share in roughly 10 of 14 markets, often with no significant national competition — these are expansion targets; (2) the chain is concentrated in the Southeast and Pacific Northwest while major markets (Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, Southwest) are untapped. Strong candidates will discuss acquisition vs. organic build and factors for selecting new expansion markets.

questions.prompt: What new products or services could the car wash company offer to grow their revenues?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm across feasibility tiers. Most feasible: add full-service options (wax, polish, undercarriage wash, detailing, coin-operated vacuums), add retail area (air fresheners, seat covers, convenience items). Medium feasibility: gas station, basic vehicle maintenance (oil changes, tire replacement), pick-up/drop-off services. Least feasible: coin-operated pet-washing area, franchise fast food (e.g., Dunkin Donuts, Subway).

questions.prompt: The team has the following information on new services. Calculate the additional revenue from: (a) adding coin-operated vacuums at $0.50 when customers vacuum half as often as they wash, and (b) adding wax services, given that low-frequency customers (10x/year, 25% of revenues) will pay $3 for wax and high-frequency customers (30x/year, 75% of revenues) will only pay $1 for wax. Will these additions achieve the 30% growth target?
questions.guidance: Candidate must work through each service's incremental revenue, then sum to check against the $12M gap (30% of $40M). At $1 wax pricing everyone uses it (including high-freq), yielding the best scenario. Even in the best case (vacuums + $1 wax), the total incremental revenue is only $10M, reaching 25% growth — 5 percentage points short of the 30% target.

math.setup: Current revenue = $40M; target = $40M × 1.30 = $52M; gap = $12M. Current washes = $40M / $5 = 8M washes/year.
steps: Vacuums: customers vacuum half as often as they wash → 8M × 50% = 4M vacuum uses; 4M × $0.50 = $2M incremental
Wax at $3 (low-freq only): low-freq revenue = $40M × 25% = $10M; at $5/wash → 2M washes; 2M × $3 = $6M incremental
Wax at $1 (all customers buy): this represents 20% of $5 wash price, and everyone uses it → $40M × 20% = $8M incremental
Best scenario (vacuums + $1 wax): $2M + $8M = $10M incremental → total revenue = $50M = 25% growth
Gap to 30% target: $52M − $50M = $2M still needed (5 percentage points short)
math.answer: Adding vacuums ($0.50) and waxing ($1) achieves only 25% revenue growth, falling 5 percentage points short of the 30% target. Additional growth levers (e.g., new markets or new services) are needed to close the gap.

brainstorming.prompt: What new products or services could the car wash company offer to grow their revenues?

categories.name: Most Feasible
ideas: Add full-service options: wax, polish, undercarriage wash, detailing
Install coin-operated vacuums in self-serve area after the wash
Add a retail area selling air fresheners, seat covers, and convenience items

categories.name: Medium Feasibility
ideas: Add a gas station to select larger locations
Offer basic vehicle maintenance: oil changes, tire replacements
Launch pick-up and drop-off car wash services

categories.name: Least Feasible
ideas: Install coin-operated pet-washing area (compete with Petco)
Add a franchise fast food outlet (e.g., Dunkin Donuts, Subway)

recommendation: The PE firm should proceed with further due diligence on the acquisition. Our analysis identified 25% revenue growth through adding vacuum and wax services to existing locations, leaving a 5-percentage-point gap to the 30% target.

The chain is the market leader in roughly 10 of 14 markets and has no national-chain competition in several of those markets, while entire major geographies (Midwest, Mid-Atlantic, Northeast, Southwest) remain untapped — providing a credible path to close the remaining gap.
risks: Entering markets with strong incumbent competitors could be costly and trigger price wars
Driving competitors out of existing markets may provoke a retaliatory price war that erodes margins
Cost analysis of adding new services has not yet been completed and could affect net returns
Rapid geographic expansion may over-extend management capacity
next_steps: Research potential new markets to enter and size the revenue opportunity in each
Dive deeper into existing markets to quantify growth potential from acquiring or displacing local competitors
Complete cost analysis of the proposed vacuum and wax service additions
Negotiate acquisition price based on the updated revenue projections
